cited_details.statement: Aphasia alone, an acquired language impairment following brain damage, affects approximately one third of people who have a stroke [https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.cd000425.pub4].

In children, SSD represent a large proportion of speech and language therapists' (SLTs) caseloads, and clinical practice surveys have documented widespread but heterogeneous use of articulatory versus phonologically based intervention approaches [https://doi.org/10.1177/0265659014550420].

The Cochrane systematic review by Brady and colleagues remains a foundational evidence synthesis for speech and language therapy (SLT) in post-stroke aphasia, evaluating randomized trials across expression, comprehension, reading, and writing modalities [https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.cd000425.pub4].

At the pediatric end of the spectrum, a national survey of Portuguese SLTs' clinical practice with children presenting phonologically based SSD documented that SSD represent a large fraction of SLT caseloads and that a wide range of articulatory-based and phonologically based approaches are applied to children with different SSD profiles [https://doi.org/10.1177/0265659014550420].

A 2022 study developed a system for acoustic data analysis aimed at assisting the diagnosis and classification of children's SSDs, with a focus on identifying and categorizing four distinct types of SSD [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9324778/].

A key finding from primary work in this area is that, although there are many online commercial CAPT apps, there is no consensus among Speech Language Therapists (SLPs) or non-professionals about which CAPT systems, if any, work well [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5884147/].

Hair and colleagues investigated ASR performance on disordered child speech using limited training data and mobile-device-friendly techniques, focusing on verifying pronunciation targets [https://psi.engr.tamu.edu/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/hair2019evaluating.pdf].

Shahin and colleagues developed an automated tool for the assessment of childhood apraxia of speech consisting of three integrated components: a clinician interface, a mobile application, and a speech processing engine [https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0167639315000382].

A research evaluation of a mobile speech therapy application reported that such apps can be suitable tools for children with apraxia and speech disorders, allowing users to select target phonemes and progress through structured practice [http://jmr.tums.ac.ir/index.php/jmr/article/download/133/80].

Das and colleagues introduced a system for stuttering speech disfluency prediction that uses explainable attribution vectors of facial muscle movements, leveraging facial kinematics in addition to acoustic information [https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.01231].

The wav2vec 2.0 framework demonstrated that learning powerful representations from speech audio alone, followed by fine-tuning on transcribed speech, can outperform previous semi-supervised methods [https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/wav2vec-2.0%3A-A-Framework-for-Self-Supervised-of-Baevski-Zhou/49a049dc85e2380dde80501a984878341dd8efdf].

Building on wav2vec 2.0 and successor models, a primary study evaluated representations from pre-trained state-of-the-art self-supervised models across three downstream tasks on dysarthric speech: disease classification, word recognition, and intelligibility classification, and under three noise scenarios on the UA-Speech dataset [https://arxiv.org/html/2306.04337v2].

Ronanki and colleagues presented a system for automatic pronunciation evaluation and mispronunciation detection using CMUSphinx, trained on a database of native exemplar pronunciations and non-native examples of frequent mistakes, and employing adaptation techniques to model learner errors [https://aclanthology.org/W12-5808.pdf].

A 2020 systematic review following PRISMA guidelines synthesized studies using speech samples obtained in the clinic or remotely to identify the presence or severity of disorders within the DSM-5 framework [https://doi.org/10.1002/lio2.354].

First, foundational self-supervised models such as wav2vec 2.0 [https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/wav2vec-2.0%3A-A-Framework-for-Self-Supervised-of-Baevski-Zhou/49a049dc85e2380dde80501a984878341dd8efdf] have become the dominant starting point for clinical speech AI, enabling transfer learning that mitigates the chronic problem of small clinical datasets, as demonstrated in the dysarthria context where HuBERT was identified as the most versatile feature extractor across classification, word recognition, and intelligibility tasks [https://arxiv.org/html/2306.04337v2].

Third, mobile and app-based delivery, exemplified by the integrated clinician interface, mobile application, and speech processing engine of the apraxia assessment tool [https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0167639315000382] and the mobile speech therapy application [http://jmr.tums.ac.ir/index.php/jmr/article/download/133/80], enables the high-frequency practice that drives neuroplastic change, but evaluation against SLT-conducted baselines remains limited.

Fourth, the field continues to lack consensus on which CAPT systems actually work for children with SSD, despite the proliferation of commercial apps [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5884147/].

Fifth, the gap between acoustic-only assessment and multimodal assessment is beginning to be addressed by incorporating visual and motor signals, as in the explainable attribution vectors of facial muscle movements used to predict stuttering disfluency [https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.01231].

ASR systems trained on adult typical speech degrade on child disordered speech, motivating the use of limited training data and mobile-device-friendly techniques in therapy applications [https://psi.engr.tamu.edu/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/hair2019evaluating.pdf].

Pronunciation evaluation systems rooted in CMUSphinx and adaptation techniques for non-native error modeling [https://aclanthology.org/W12-5808.pdf] have provided a methodological foundation, but their clinical extension to disordered speech remains an active research area.

Automated speech analysis has demonstrated broad applicability to clinical assessment beyond communication disorders, including psychiatric assessment via DSM-5 [https://doi.org/10.1002/lio2.354], suggesting that the methodological pipeline developed for speech therapy may also inform adjacent clinical domains.
